newsitem.title: USA: Chicago Fed's Moskow supports preemptive policy.
newsitem.headline: Chicago Fed's Moskow supports preemptive policy.

text.p: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago President Michael Moskow said on Thursday the U.S. central bank must have a preemptive policy to foil inflationary pressures that may threaten the economy's long-term growth.

"The Fed tightened policy in 1994 to eliminate inflationary pressures that were building," Moskow told the Chicago Chapter of the Industrial Relations Research Association. "I think it was absolutely the right move."
Moskow echoed Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan, who in his recent Humphrey-Hawkins testimony defended the 1994 tightening cycle and the need for Fed policy to be preemptive.

"The Fed acted to head off inflationary pressures before they became a problem," Moskow added. "This forward-looking approach is necessary because of the lags in monetary policy. Monetary policy is like a time-release capsule."
Moskow, acknowledging that such policy may draw criticism, stressed "the key is balancing short-term gains against long-term benefits."
Reflecting on past Fed policy, Moskow further emphasized the benefits of deflating inflationary pressures "instead of waiting and bursting the balloon after the fact."
"We learned in the late 1970s that waiting is too painful," the Chicago Fed president added.
Turning to the U.S. economy's long-term, sustainable rate of growth, Moskow said it is a function of "population growth, technological advances and productivity improvements."
Moskow reiterated that the best contribution the Fed can make to help the economy steadily grow at its potential rate is by ensuring price stability.

"The Fed is all about growth. We want the highest possible level of growth and jobs that can be sustained," Moskow stated. "The only effective way for a central bank to do that in the long run is to foster price stability."
